generator.params.apical.why: A fir, spruce, hemlock or Douglas-fir holds its branches under its leader (apical control): each year a branch grows about half as far as the leader rises, so the crown is a cone about as wide as its depth, and stays pointed as the leader slows.

generator.params.bend_set.why: The family's limbs spring back from most of each year's sag: Farjon gives its branches as horizontal or spreading, the lower ones curving down only at their ends. Keeping half of each year's sag, a limb grown 150 years hung flat against the trunk and the old crown stood as a column.

generator.params.side_order.why: An old fir, spruce, hemlock or Douglas-fir keeps its limbs leafy by branching them again and again: second-order shoots set twigs of their own, so a limb ends in a dense fan of foliage. Branching only once, every old crown was a fishbone of bare whips with needles at their tips.

generator.params.twig_years.why: The twigs on a limb's side shoots live about as long as their needles and are replaced from below; kept for ever, the fully branched crown passed the program's module limit before 200 years.

generator.params.epi_years.why: A limb's dormant buds wait as long as the limb lives and resprout it where light reaches them: old Douglas-fir crowns keep their foliage by such epicormic shoots (Ishii & Ford 2001), as old firs, spruces and hemlocks reiterate theirs. Living 80 years, the buds were spent before the crown aged, and old crowns lost three quarters of their foliage between 150 and 300 years.

generator.params.epi_light.why: A limb's dormant buds sprout where a little light reaches them, in the shaded lower crown as well as the lit top: Ishii & Ford (2001) find epicormic shoots in every part of old Douglas-fir crowns, and on some lower-crown limbs nearly half the shoots and foliage epicormic. Needing 0.3 of the open sky's light, a bud sprouted only near the top, where few limbs are bare.

generator.params.epi_order.why: The dormant buds that resprout an old limb wait along its main axis, where its epicormic shoots stand (Ishii & Ford 2001); buds kept on every side shoot as well filled the program's module limit before 300 years.

generator.params.branch_floor.why: Once the leader slows, a lit limb still lengthens, by up to 15 cm a year near the stem in full light and less with its reach and its shade, so an old crown keeps renewing its foliage where it is lit, and widening out to floor_reach, instead of stopping where the leader did. The floor comes in over the top floor_ramp share of the height, so the top whorls stay short and the top pointed.

generator.params.bud_keep.why: A tip's new shoot shortens as the tree's rise slows, so an old crown's tips shade one another less than a sapling's vigorous ones: each keeps a fifth of a fast-rising tip's shade once the leader has stopped. Shading as much as a sapling's, an old crown starved inside.

generator.params.apical_light.why: Shade strengthens apical control: a shaded branch takes a smaller share of the leader's shoot than a lit one, so a tree grown in a stand keeps a narrow crown while its leader races up (forest-grown Douglas-fir about 3 m across its crown at 30 years, its trunk about 25 cm through). Taking the full share in any light, the shaded limbs of a stand-grown Douglas-fir spread 4 m and carried four times the needles, and its trunk grew twice as thick as stand-grown trees'.

generator.params.side_floor.why: Once the leader stops rising, a limb's side shoots still grow a few centimetres a year and set twigs, renewing the foliage along it. Held to the leader's dwindling growth with the limb's own tip, they shrank to millimetres and set almost no twigs, and old crowns lost their foliage after 150 years (grand fir, Douglas-fir, western hemlock).

generator.params.floor_ramp.why: The side shoots' floor comes in over the top 15% of an old tree's height (in metres, 10 m left a 20 m subalpine fir's top half as bare limbs carrying sprays only at their tips), so its top stays narrow: in full to the treetop, the short limbs of an old tree's top whorls carried side shoots longer than themselves, and the tops of 300-year Douglas-fir, Sitka spruce and subalpine fir were domes two to four times as wide as photographed ones (inaturalist-crowns-2026-10: the top tenth .06 to .12 of the height).

generator.params.floor_reach.why: An old crown stops widening once its height slows: its shoots' floor growth fades past a tenth of the tree's height out from the trunk, down to floor_keep, so the limbs' ends still renew their foliage but no longer carry the crown outward. Branch growth goes on in old Douglas-fir after the tree stops rising and its crown stops spreading, so the crown turns cylindrical, deep and irregular, its lower half held by epicormic shoots (Ishii and McDowell 2002, 450-year trees at Wind River). With the floor fading only in columnar crowns, a Douglas-fir grown 480 years in a stand drew a dome 21 m across over bare limbs: the top whorls, born as its leader slowed, lengthened for two centuries until the top was as wide as the crown, and 99% of its foliage stood in the top fifth of its height, the lower half of the foliated crown holding 9%. With it the crown is 18 m across, foliated from 62 down to 37 m, and that lower half holds 35%, though it holds less foliage (355 m² against 414) on a thinner trunk (74 cm against 86), the pipe model's trunk following its crown; western hemlock's dome at 480 years goes the same way (18% to 40%). Every Pinaceae species' young sizes stay within a few percent of before. Columnar crowns took it first: without it, a 300-year subalpine fir (FEIS: an extremely narrow crown of short branches) grew to .64 of its height across against the photographed old tree's .37, its sides spreading every year after its leader slowed at 60 years; with it, .44 (seed 1), its foliage thinning from 540 m² at 60 years to 350 at 300 as the photographed old trees' crowns go ragged, and its 15- and 60-year crown widths unchanged (60-year leaf area 670 to 540 m², dbh 42 to 39 cm).

generator.params.floor_keep_limb.why: Past floor_reach an old limb's own axis stops lengthening while its side shoots keep floor_keep and renew its foliage, so the crown stops spreading once the tree stops rising. With every axis keeping floor_keep, a few upper limbs crept outward for three centuries and a 480-year Douglas-fir grown in a stand spread 12 m from its trunk, where the Forest Vegetation Simulator's crown-width equation for a tree of its size gives about 6.5 m; with side shoots stopped too, an old western hemlock lost a quarter of its foliage and its lower crown.

generator.params.limb_light.why: An old limb is shed for want of light only when its tips catch little light for the wood they carry, a third as readily as the pines' 0.01: a fully branched old limb carries many segments, and at 0.01 limbs whose foliage was well lit were shed for their size, so subalpine fir and western larch lost four fifths of their foliage between 150 and 300 years.

generator.params.limb_tip.why: A limb older than limb_age whose tips' mean light has fallen to the starving point is shed whatever its size, as a shaded limb dies once its foliage no longer pays for it (branch autonomy): with the per-segment rule eased, shaded limbs would otherwise linger and fill the program's module limit.

generator.params.seg_min.why: An old limb's slow shoots, a centimetre or two a year, are laid down as one shoot every few years with the same needle area, so a fully branched old crown keeps its side shoots within the program's module and segment limits: laid down every year, old Douglas-fir and western hemlock passed them unless their inner side shoots were shed or cut short (side_years), which left their lower limbs bare whips. Young shoots, longer than 4 cm a year, grow as before. Not 8 cm: a held shoot's spray is as large as its years' together and a spray draws its needles a share of its length, so at 8 cm the median drawn needle passed the floras' extremes (Douglas-fir 4.0 cm against 2 to 3, grand fir 6.4 against 3.5 to 5); at 4 cm, with a held shoot's foliage drawn at two places along it (pinidae), Douglas-fir draws 3.4 cm over three plants.

generator.params.seg_side.why: An old tree's side shoots hold their growth until they reach 20 cm and lay it down as one shoot, drawing its foliage at one place for each three years held: an old crown's side shoots grow a centimetre or two a year for a century and more, and four fifths of their 4 cm segments were bare wood older than twenty years (a 320-year Douglas-fir grown in a stand: 344,000 segments, 317,000 of them side shoots), so a 500-year Douglas-fir at a stand's edge passed the program's 2 million segment limit near 400 years. With it (from seg_age) the edge tree has 1.02 million segments at 500 years, and a 480-year Douglas-fir in a stand 258,000 (724,000 before) with 844 m² of foliage (757). 12 cm left the edge tree at 1.5 million. The pines lay down every year's shoot (seg_min 0) and are unchanged.

generator.params.seg_age.why: seg_side comes in from 100 years and is in full by 200, so young trees grow as before: a held shoot's needles appear only when it is laid down, and young trees' foliage is mostly on their side shoots, so from the first year 20 cm took two fifths of a 60-year western hemlock's and grand fir's foliage and a quarter of a Douglas-fir's. An old crown is short of light more than of needles: at 480 years the Douglas-fir holds more foliage with it, not less.

generator.params.bud_length.why: A shoot shorter than 10 cm sets proportionally fewer side buds, so a slow old crown no longer smothers itself in buds (pinidae revision 13); set for the family, as the yews and cypresses it was not fitted on branch as before.

generator.params.top_ramp.why: Branch shoots are shortest in the top whorls and lengthen over the first few whorls below the treetop (Cannell et al. 1976, Sitka spruce), so the top is a point: at full length from the first year, young treetops were three to five times as wide as photographed ones. Counted in years of the leader's growth, not metres: over a fixed 2 m, a 16 m subalpine fir's whorls born as its leader slowed to about 15 cm a year stayed stubs for a decade, leaving a bare stretch of leader under a tuft (widths at 0.85 and 0.95 of the height .06 and .04 at 60 years, photographed young trees .12 and .05); over 4 years they draw .14 and .06, and mountain hemlock's lollipop top goes too. Fitted on the seven Pinaceae with photographs at 15 and 60 years: 4 years matched as well as or better than 2 m for all but Sitka spruce at 15 (profile error .12 to .15); 6 years widened young tops.

generator.params.ring_share.why: Once the leader passes half its full height, each square metre of foliage lays down less trunk wood, as (half the full height / height) squared, as taller trees grow less stem for their leaf area (Ryan and Yoder 1997, hydraulic limitation): with the same ring area per leaf at every height, 300-year open-grown trees drew trunks two to three times the floras' (Douglas-fir 5.2 m against Abrams' 1 to 3.5 m and FEIS's 1.5 to 1.8 m common in old growth; grand fir 3.0 m against 1 to 1.5 m, up to 2). Tried at 0.45 and 0.6, 300-year Douglas-fir drew 3.1 and 3.8 m, grand fir 1.7 and 2.1 m, Sitka spruce 2.1 and 2.7 m (to 5 m, Abrams), and the 60-year sizes stayed within 4% of before; 0.5 is between them.

generator.params.stem_epi.why: Old trees renew their crowns from dormant buds on the trunk: in 450-year Douglas-firs the lower crown is mostly epicormic branches, several from one small patch of stem, younger and smaller than the original limbs about them, which reiterate the tree's young form (Ishii and McDowell 2002). A stem bud left at each whorl sprouts with chance 0.1 a year once the leader's rise is under a quarter of its fastest, where a twentieth of the open sky's light reaches it, as a limb three times a young limb's vigour. Genera whose limbs' buds do not sprout (epi_chance 0, the pines) keep none on the stem either.

generator.params.stem_epi_light.why: A stem bud sprouts where a twentieth of the open sky's light reaches it: the lower crown of an old Douglas-fir is mostly epicormic (Ishii and McDowell 2002), in deep shade under its own crown.

generator.params.stem_epi_vigour.why: A stem sprout grows as a young limb does: epicormic branches fill an old Douglas-fir's crown from within and stay short (Ishii and McDowell 2002; Sillett et al. 2018: old crowns narrow, with few long branches). At three times a limb's vigour, sprouts set from 150 years on reached out 10 m by 250 years, doubling a stand-grown Douglas-fir's crown radius where the Forest Vegetation Simulator's crown-width equation gives about 5.5 m.

generator.params.shade_own.why: A needle grown in shade carries less mass per area than one in the sun, by the light at its own shoot: down an old Douglas-fir's crown its specific needle area rises steadily with depth, and its shaded lower-crown and epicormic shoots are the cheapest (Ishii et al. 2002), as an understorey silver fir's needle mass per area falls with the light at its apex (King 1997). So a shoot shaded by its own crown, not only one on a plant shaded all over, pays the shade needle's lower cost, and an old crown keeps foliage deeper down.

generator.params.top_die.why: Storms and dieback take old trees' tops, and new leaders (reiterated trunks) rise from the break: Douglas-fir crowns stay simple, as their architectural model has them, until damaged, few trees under 300 years carry reiterated trunks, and many older ones do (Sillett et al. 2018); old-growth trees 'often have multiple or dead tops' (Franklin and Spies). Once the leader's yearly rise is under a twentieth of its fastest (about 215 years in a Douglas-fir), it dies with chance 0.002 a year: about one tree in six by 300 years and two in five by 480.

generator.params.top_rise.why: A top dies only once the tree has nearly stopped rising (its leader's yearly rise under a twentieth of its fastest): Sillett et al.'s (2018) Cascade Douglas-firs under 300 years kept model-conforming crowns.

rules.note: Old conifers (pinidae revision 13): apical control as Wilson (2000) describes it, the leader holding its branches' growth below its own. A branch's yearly shoot is a share of the leader's, so a whorl's branches lengthen as the leader above them rises and the crown is a cone. With a fixed yearly length instead, the crowns stood as tubes whose top halves were twice as wide as photographed open-grown trees' (inaturalist-crowns-2026-10); 0.5 is the middle of the six species fitted to those photographs, 0.36 to 0.6. bend_set 0.15 (the same revision): at the Pinidae's 0.5, grand fir and western hemlock grown 150 years carried their limbs hanging against the trunk; at 0.15 grand fir's old crown stays conical. Ramifying old crowns (the same revision): side_order 2 with twigs that live twig_years 10 and dormant buds that live epi_years 80 keep old limbs leafy, as Strieby's (2017) Sitka spruce plate and the old trees photographed show, within the module limit to 300 years (twigs carry one spray of the three's area). branch_floor 0.06 and top_ramp 2 (Cannell et al. 1976) fitted with each species' apical and branch_reach to the same photographs at 15, 60, 150 and 300 years. Old crowns (pinidae revision 14): bud_keep 0.2, branch_floor 0.15 coming in over floor_ramp, and epi_light 0.1, fitted together so a Douglas-fir grown 250 years in a stand holds about half the leaf area Sillett et al.'s (2018) equation gives for its crown volume and diameter (288 m², 44% of a crown now 26 m deep, where it held 163 m², 29%), and a western hemlock grown alike 253 m² (177 before; 64% of the Douglas-fir equation), while every species of the family keeps its reference sizes at 30 to 60 years. With branch_floor 0.15 in full to the treetop, both grew flat tops as broad as their crowns over bare limbs. Old crowns stop spreading (the same revision): floor_reach 0.1 for every crown of the family, not only columnar ones, as Ishii and McDowell (2002) find old Douglas-fir crowns cylindrical; at 480 years the Douglas-fir and hemlock crowns had turned to domes over bare limbs without it.

traits.note: Abrams (vol. 1, 1923, p. 52), Pinaceae: resinous trees whose linear or needle-like leaves are set in spirals; pollen and seed cones on the same tree; the seed cone woody, ripening in its first or second season.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 150, family Pinaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral; read as "spiral".

traits.leaf_division.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 150, family Pinaceae: leaf division simple; read as "simple".

traits.leaf_habit.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 150, family Pinaceae: leaf habit evergreen (deciduous in Larix and Pseudolarix), usually. Read together as {"evergreen": "usually", "deciduous": "rarely"}.

traits.reproduction.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 151, 152, 153, family Pinaceae: reproduction cones; read as "cones".

rules.generator.params.stem_epi.note: Ishii and McDowell (2002), Forest Ecology and Management 169: 257-270: in 450-year Wind River Douglas-firs the lower crown is extended by epicormic branches from the main stem, 13 to 57.5% of the lower half's branch volume; several arise from a small patch of stem and are younger and smaller than the original branches near them. Chance, light and vigour fitted to Sillett et al. (2018) Table 7 (about 630 m2 a Douglas-fir at 480 years, 1,240-1,480 at 550-650).

rules.generator.params.shade_own.note: Ishii et al. (2002), Tree Physiology 22: 31-40: in old-growth Wind River Douglas-firs, specific needle area increased linearly with decreasing height in the crown, about 0.95 cm2/g per metre, and epicormic shoots carried the highest; foliage is renewed in the lower crown by epicormic shoots. The cost's form is King (1997, Tree Physiology 17: 251-258; pinidae revision 17's shade_cost): needle mass per area 130 + 185 times the light at the apex, g/m2. Checked against Ishii and McDowell (2002): 450-year crowns' live crown ratio 0.64.

rules.generator.params.floor_keep_limb.note: FVS Staff (2008, revised 2026), Pacific Northwest Coast (PN) variant overview of the Forest Vegetation Simulator, equation 4.4.5 with Crookston's (2005) Douglas-fir coefficients (20205): forest-grown crown width = 6.0227 x BF x DBH^0.54361 x HT^-0.20669 x CL^0.20395 x (BA+1)^-0.00644 x exp(EL)^-0.00378 (feet, inches), about 11 m across for a 250-year stand-grown Douglas-fir (80 cm, 63 m) and 13 m for a 480-year one (134-142 cm). Sillett et al. (2018): tall old Douglas-firs have narrow crowns.

rules.generator.params.top_die.note: Sillett et al. (2018), Forest Ecology and Management 429: 93-114, 60 climbed Douglas-firs: trees under 100 years (Olympic) and 300 years (Cascade) had model-conforming crowns with few if any trunk reiterations; older trees had reiterated trunks and individualized structure, though some over 300 years kept simple crowns; 'decapitation of treetops and branch tips in storms eventually leads to trunk reiteration'. Their Fig. 3 shows reiterated trunks near the top in about a third (Cascade) to a half (Olympic) of the old trees. Rate fitted to those shares.

rules.generator.params.top_rise.note: Sillett et al. (2018): Cascade Douglas-firs under 300 years kept model-conforming crowns, with few if any reiterated trunks; a twentieth of the fastest rise is reached at about 215 years by the Douglas-fir's height curve.
